title: Can Testimonial Learning be Considered Rational?: Revisions, Extensions, and New Insights to a Theory of Selective Trust
abstract: Abstract Numerous studies have shown that children selectively learn from others’ testimony and are not indiscriminately trusting of all social interaction. Thirteen years ago, we published a paper (Sobel & Kushnir, 2013) that introduced a theory of selective trust in testimony grounded in rational learning mechanisms similar to those we developed with our mentor, Alison Gopnik, to explain children's causal reasoning and theory change. In honor of Alison receiving the Rumelhart Award, we take the opportunity to engage with our original claims, update them in light of new evidence, and propose ways to integrate the rational framework with new ideas in the field. We begin with a review of two recent meta‐analyses that support the rational learning account. We then consider new data showing that testimony enhances processing of children's own observations and actions and discuss how this data might lead to extensions of our theory. We next revisit and modify our original claims about “emotional trust” and suggest that affiliative motives which conflict with truth‐seeking motives may alter, or even undermine, the rational learning process. We end with new directions for selective trust research: examining developmental changes from infancy, integrating more cultural influences, and considering the role of selective trust in children's increasing interactions with AI and other technology.
